exercises.prompt: `use Data::Report;` searches each directory in `@INC` for a file. What is that file's path relative to the directory? (For example, `Text::Tally` is `Text/Tally.pm`.)
exercises.solution: `Data::Report` becomes `Data/Report.pm`: the double colons map to directories and `.pm` is added. If a directory in `@INC` is `lib`, Perl looks for `lib/Data/Report.pm`, and records where it found it in `%INC`.

exercises.prompt: Which is exactly equivalent to `use Text::Tally qw(word_counts);`?

options.label: `BEGIN { require Text::Tally; Text::Tally->import(qw(word_counts)); }`
options.feedback: Yes. `use` loads the module and calls its `import` method, both at compile time.

options.label: `require Text::Tally; Text::Tally->import(qw(word_counts));` at the point where the line appears, at run time
options.feedback: Not yet. That is what the lesson's program did by hand, but `use` happens at compile time, inside a `BEGIN` block, before the rest of the file runs.

options.label: `do 'Text/Tally.pm';`
options.feedback: Not yet. `do FILE` runs a file every time it is called, does not check `%INC` to avoid reloading, and does not import anything.

options.label: `package Text::Tally;`
options.feedback: Not yet. `package` switches the current namespace; it does not load any file.

hints: `use` does two things: load and import.
When does a `use` statement take effect, compared with the code around it?
exercises.solution: `use Module LIST` is `BEGIN { require Module; Module->import(LIST); }`. `require` finds and loads the file once (recording it in `%INC`), `import` lets the module put names into your package, and `BEGIN` makes both happen at compile time.

feedback.message: Not yet. `play` calls `$self->sound`, and for a Drum object Perl finds Drum's own `sound` first.

hints: `Drum` has no `play`, so Perl uses Instrument's.
Inside `play`, which `sound` does `$self->sound` find when `$self` is a Drum?
exercises.solution: `Drum->new` uses Instrument's `new`, which blesses into `Drum`. `play` is inherited, but inside it `$self->sound` looks up `sound` starting from the object's own class, Drum, so it gets `boom`. The Instrument object gets the base `sound`. The lines are `Kofi plays boom` and `Mei plays a note`.

hints: Any reference can be blessed, not only hashes.
`ref` on a blessed reference returns the class name; on an unblessed one, the kind of reference.
exercises.solution: `bless [], 'Queue'` makes an array reference into an object of class Queue, so `ref` returns `Queue`, and `isa('Queue')` is true (1). A plain `[]` is not blessed, so `ref` returns `ARRAY`. Output: `Queue 1 ARRAY`.

hints: `SUPER::hello` means the parent of the package where the *calling method* was defined.
Follow the calls: Top, then Mid, then Base.
exercises.solution: `Top->new` inherits `new` from Base and blesses into Top. `Top::hello` calls `SUPER::hello`, which is Mid's; `Mid::hello` calls its `SUPER::hello`, which is Base's, returning `base`. The pieces join on the way back: `top+mid+base`.

Tickets are numbered in the order they were made.
exercises.solution: There is one `$issued` variable, shared by every call to `new`, whichever class it is called on. Two Tickets and three VipTickets make five, so `Ticket->issued` is 5. The last VipTicket was the fifth ticket made, so its number is 5. The sum is 10.

exercises.prompt: A team is starting a Perl service that uses several CPAN modules. Which practices are sound? Choose all that apply.

options.label: List dependencies in a `cpanfile` and commit Carton's `cpanfile.snapshot`
options.feedback: Yes. The snapshot records exact versions, so every machine installs the same set.

options.label: Install modules into the operating system's Perl with `sudo cpan`
options.feedback: Not yet. The system Perl belongs to the operating system; changing its modules can break system tools, and upgrades can break your service.

options.label: Before adopting a module, check its latest release, CPAN Testers results and reverse dependencies on MetaCPAN
options.feedback: Yes. These are quick signals of whether a module is maintained and trusted.

options.label: Use a separate Perl (perlbrew, plenv or a container) or install into a project directory with `cpanm -L local`
options.feedback: Yes. Keeping the project's Perl and modules separate from the system's avoids conflicts.

hints: Who else depends on the system Perl?
What makes an installation reproducible on another machine?
exercises.solution: Pin dependencies with a cpanfile and a committed snapshot, vet modules on MetaCPAN, and keep your Perl and modules separate from the operating system's. Installing into the system Perl with sudo risks breaking both the system and the service.
